section.title: Careers
section.intro: What the work is actually like, and which door leads to it. Every one of these has more than one way in, whatever the person who holds it tells you.

items.title: Electrician
items.subtitle: Trades
items.summary: Paid from your first year, no fees, qualified in four. Then you can work for anyone or nobody.
items.body:
Electricians install, maintain and repair electrical systems. Houses, sites, factories, and increasingly solar panels, heat pumps and car chargers. There is a formal qualification at the end of it and exams that people fail, so treat anyone describing it as unskilled labour as telling you more about them than about the job.

Once you are qualified you can work for a company, work for yourself, or end up running the site rather than being on it.

routes.name: Apprenticeship
routes.detail: Find an employer, they register you, and you alternate between working for them and blocks of training. You are on the payroll throughout.

routes.name: PLC first, then apprenticeship
routes.detail: A year of electrical training makes an employer far likelier to take you. Common route for anyone who came out of sixth year with nothing lined up.

routes.name: Later on
routes.detail: People start this at twenty-eight after five years of something they disliked. It is allowed.

blocks.heading: What you need
blocks.text: A Leaving Certificate at a basic grade level, or an approved equivalent, or an employer who wants you anyway. Maths and a practical subject help. High points are not the currency here. Check the current entry requirements rather than taking this paragraph as gospel.

blocks.heading: What you earn on the way
blocks.text: A percentage of the qualified rate from year one, rising each year. You finish owing nothing, having been paid for four years. Compare that with the alternative honestly and not sentimentally.

myths.myth: It's what you do if you're not academic.
myths.reality: The exams fail people. Different difficulty, not a lesser one.
It helps, which is why this site exists. Ringing round local firms also works, and hardly anyone bothers.
Supervision, contracting, inspection, teaching, your own company. Some of them earn more than the people who looked down on it.

items.title: Software developer
items.subtitle: Technology
items.summary: One of the few well-paid jobs where nobody asks about your degree after the first one.
items.body:
Developers write the code behind apps and systems. The job is less solitary than films suggest. Most of the day goes on reading other people's code, arguing about what to build, and repairing things that worked yesterday.

Ireland has far more of this work than you'd expect for a country this size, across both the large foreign companies and a lot of Irish ones nobody has heard of.

routes.name: Computer science degree
routes.detail: Three or four years through the CAO. Strongest grounding, and the simplest way into the graduate programmes the bigger employers recruit through.
routes.cost: Student contribution, often covered by SUSI

routes.name: Apprenticeship
routes.detail: Software and ICT apprenticeships exist here and hardly anyone mentions them. You work, you study alongside it, you come out with a qualification and real years behind you.

routes.name: PLC, then work or a degree
routes.detail: A computing course in further education leads to junior roles directly, or into a degree through links with the universities.

routes.name: Teaching yourself
routes.detail: It happens, and this industry does care more about what you can build than where you sat. But there is no structure, nobody to ask, and you need finished work to show. Easier as a second career than a first job.

blocks.heading: What you need
blocks.text: Points for computing courses vary enormously, and there are options well down the range, not only at the top. Maths helps and some courses require it, but it is less of a wall than people assume. Apprenticeships and further education ask for a lot less. Check the specific course.

blocks.heading: What it pays
blocks.text: Entry salaries in this sector are high compared with most other first jobs in Ireland and they move quickly in the early years. The apprenticeship route pays from the start.

myths.myth: You need to have been coding since you were twelve.
myths.reality: Plenty of working developers started at eighteen. Or thirty. Early helps, it is not a requirement.
Some courses want it, many do not, and most of the day-to-day work uses very little of it.

myths.myth: It has to be a well-known university.
myths.reality: After your first job nobody asks. What you have built is the whole conversation.
